power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Beyond Behavioral Signs: Toward a Multidomain Risk Architecture for Early Detection of Autism Spectrum Disorder

text.text: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) prevalence has increased markedly over recent decades, yet primary tools for early detection remain focused almost exclusively on observable behavioral signs in children aged 18 months and older.

Instruments such as the M-CHAT-R/F, ADOS-2, and ADI-R, while clinically valuable, operate within a narrow temporal and conceptual window that systematically excludes a wide range of prenatal, perinatal, medical, environmental, and psychosocial signals now supported by robust empirical evidence.
Objective: This paper presents a theoretically grounded critique of current early detection frameworks for ASD and proposes a Multidomain Early Risk Architecture (MERA).

MERA is a detection architecture rather than a causal model of aetiology: it organizes ten empirically supported domains of clinically accessible signals according to the developmental window in which each becomes observable, and specifies through a four-tier taxonomy what inference each class of signal can bear.
Approach: A structured narrative synthesis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2006 and 2025 was conducted across PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science.
Each retained source was mapped to one of 75 candidate risk factors and classified by study design and journal indexing quartile.
The resulting evidence base comprises 152 factor-source pairings drawn from 148 distinct sources, organized into ten thematic domains and four evidential tiers.
Findings: The retained literature documents ASD-relevant signals distributed across all ten domains and four developmental windows.
Sixty-nine percent of pairings derive from quartile-1 Page 1 journals and 38 from systematic reviews or meta-analyses.
Half of the evidence base corresponds to factors established before any behavioural observation of the child is possible, and which no current screening instrument incorporates.

Domains differ systematically in evidential status: some comprise antecedent exposures, others early prodromal markers, and others features of the diagnostic phenotype itself or associated conditions of contested directionality.
Conclusion: A multidomain architecture that stratifies signals by developmental window and by evidential status offers a conceptual foundation for tiered developmental surveillance.
The framework has implications for instrument development, primary care protocols, and public health policy-particularly in settings such as Chile where diagnostic delays remain substantial.
Its domain structure and clinical utility require prospective validation, which the framework is explicitly designed to enable.
The global prevalence of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has undergone a profound transformation over recent decades.

Where rates once hovered around 1 in 150 children, recent surveillance data from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimate 1 in 36 children as of 2023, with similar upward trends across Europe, Australia, East Asia, and Latin America.
This trajectory reflects not only improved diagnostic sensitivity but a genuine broadening of the phenotypic landscape.

In Chile, ASD has been progressively incorporated into national developmental monitoring guidelines, yet diagnostic delays in the public health system range from two to four years from first parental concern to formal diagnosis.
Against this backdrop, the dominant paradigm for early ASD detection rests on a behavioral surveillance model.

Tools such as the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers-Revised with Follow-up (M-CHAT-R/F), the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS-2), and the Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R) have become gold-standard instruments by virtue of their strong psychometric properties and clinical utility.
Yet all share a fundamental structural limitation: they are designed to identify behavioral anomalies in children already old enough to display them-typically at 18 months or later.
This temporal constraint means detection begins precisely where overt behavioral divergence becomes visible, while ignoring the complex developmental trajectory that precedes it.
A growing body of evidence challenges this behaviorally centered and temporally narrow model.

Prospective longitudinal studies of infant siblings of autistic children document divergence in canonical babbling, motor development, and social orienting within the first year of life (Long et al., 2024; Yankowitz et al., 2022; Gabis et al., 2020; Hatch et al., 2021); large-scale Nordic population registry studies report associations between ASD diagnosis and antenatal and perinatal characteristics established before birth (Persson et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2019; Villamor et al., 2022); meta-analyses of prenatal and perinatal exposures converge on a consistent set of obstetric and pharmacological associations (Garza-Martínez et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Gardener et al., 2011); and experimental neuroimaging and electrophysiological research identifies atypical neural response as early as the first postnatal months (Hazlett et al., 2017; Jones & Klin, 2013).

text.text: Taken together, these literatures indicate that signals relevant to ASD are distributed across biological, environmental, and psychosocial dimensions, and that a subset of them is detectableand, in the case of certain modifiable exposures, potentially alterable-well before the behavioral phenotype consolidates.
The theoretical implication is substantial.

If ASD risk accumulates across ten or more domains spanning the prenatal period through early childhood, instruments evaluating only behavioral signs at 18-36 months are not merely incomplete but structurally misaligned with the developmental process they seek to detect, with clinical consequences: delayed intervention, foreclosed preventive action, and systematic disadvantage for populations with limited specialist access.
This paper pursues two interconnected objectives.

The first is a theoretically grounded critique of current early detection frameworks, arguing that their behaviorally centered architecture constitutes a structural blind spot rather than a mere empirical gap.

The second is the proposal of the Multidomain Early Risk Architecture (MERA)-a conceptual framework integrating ten empirically supported domains of ASD-relevant signals into a developmentally organized structure, and specifying through a four-tier taxonomy of evidential status what inference each class of signal can support.
>Structural Limitations of Current Behavioral Detection Frameworks
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Structural Limitations of Current Behavioral Detection Frameworks</head>

text.text: The modern architecture of ASD detection was shaped by two converging forces: the progressive refinement of diagnostic criteria from DSM-III through DSM-5, and the observation that specific behavioral anomalies-particularly in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors-reliably discriminated ASD from other developmental profiles.
The resulting instruments are behaviorally anchored by design.

The M-CHAT-R/F evaluates 20 items all requiring observation of specific behaviors-pointing, gaze following, name response-that are developmentally appropriate targets only after approximately 12-18 months.
This grounding has genuine virtues: behavioral criteria are observable, relatively standardized across cultural contexts, and reliably assessed by clinicians and parents.
The problem is not that behavioral detection is wrong; it is that it is temporally and theoretically incomplete.
A clarification of scope is required.
The limitation identified here concerns instruments designed specifically for ASD detection.

General developmental surveillance-the Ages and Stages Questionnaire, the Survey of Well-being of Young Children, or periodic surveillance under paediatric guidelines-does operate from the first year and does evaluate motor, language, and social-emotional milestones.

The argument is not that such surveillance is temporally late, but that it is milestone-referenced rather than risk-stratified: it evaluates whether expected competencies have been reached at a given age, and incorporates at no point the antecedent biomedical and family-history information already held in the clinical record (see §6.3).
The behavioral model implicitly assumes that ASD emerges at or around the point at which its symptoms become visible, an assumption inconsistent with available developmental neuroscience.

Neuroimaging studies of infant siblings demonstrate structural and functional brain differences detectable as early as 6 months, preceding behavioral sign consolidation by 6-12 months (Hazlett et al., 2017); electrophysiological studies show atypical cortical responses to social and auditory stimuli at 3-4 months (Jones & Klin, 2013); and prospective studies following high-likelihood infants from birth document characteristic trajectories-reduced canonical babbling, atypical motor development, diminished social orienting-within the first year (Long et al., 2024; Gabis et al., 2020; Yankowitz et al., 2022).

text.text: Population cohort studies from Sweden, Denmark, Finland, and Norway involving millions of participants have identified robust associations between ASD diagnosis and factors present at or before birth: advanced parental age, obstetric complications, gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, prematurity, low birth weight, and prenatal exposure to pharmacological and environmental agents (Persson et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2024; Garza-Martínez et al., 2025).

text.text: These have been replicated across independent datasets and implicate epigenetic, immunological, metabolic, and neurological mechanisms operating during pregnancy and the neonatal period.
The behavioral detection model, by virtue of its temporal anchoring, is blind to this pre-behavioral period; the composition of the evidence base across domains is reported in §4.
A second structural limitation concerns the scope of the behavioral phenotype itself.

DSM-5 criteria represent a necessary simplification for diagnostic purposes, but a growing literature documents that the clinical presentation of ASD has expanded substantially beyond this core, and that many individuals who meet criteria present with profiles current instruments were not designed to capture.

Individuals previously diagnosed under other categories-social (pragmatic) communication disorder, sensory processing disorder, hyperlexia, pathological demand avoidance, specific learning disabilities-are increasingly recognized as part of the spectrum.

Presentations such as the female phenotype characterized by social camouflaging, or late-identified adults whose compensatory strategies masked difficulties, were largely invisible to instruments calibrated on male, clinically referred samples.
This expansion creates an additional detection gap: instruments designed around a modal presentation systematically under-identify those who deviate from it.
MERA is not a causal model of ASD aetiology, and it does not assert that the factors it organizes are causally implicated in ASD pathogenesis.

It is a detection architecture: a framework for organizing heterogeneous, clinically accessible signals according to the developmental window in which each becomes observable and the inferential weight each can legitimately bear.
The distinction is consequential.
An aetiological model must satisfy temporal precedence, mechanistic plausibility, and freedom from reverse causation.

A detection architecture operates under a lower requirement: it must identify signals that, alone or combined, raise the posterior probability that a child warrants comprehensive developmental assessment.
Signals that are consequences of an emerging phenotype rather than causes remain informative for detection precisely because they co-occur with it.
What they cannot support is causal inference, and MERA makes no such claim.
One qualification applies.

The framework does advance mechanistic hypotheses about why particular domains should interact-that neuroinflammatory, microbiome-mediated, and epigenetic pathways provide plausible substrates for cross-domain amplification.
These are auxiliary hypotheses whose function is to render the interactive principle testable rather than to constitute an aetiological theory, and Figure 3 should be read accordingly.

text.text: The clarification has a direct methodological implication, developed in §5.1: because the components differ in what they can be used to infer, they must be classified by evidential status rather than treated as a homogeneous set of risk factors.
>Approach to the Evidence Synthesis
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Approach to the Evidence Synthesis</head>

text.text: The evidence base was assembled through a structured narrative review, selected over a PRISMAconstrained systematic review for reasons that warrant statement.

The objective was not to estimate a pooled effect for a single exposure-outcome relationship, for which systematic review and metaanalysis are appropriate, but to construct a conceptual integration across ten heterogeneous domains whose literatures differ substantially in design, measurement, and terminology.
A protocol-constrained search optimized for one question would have fragmented rather than integrated this literature.
The tradeoff is reduced transparency of selection, revisited in §8.1.
Searches were conducted in PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science.

Search terms combined ('autism spectrum disorder' OR 'autism' OR 'ASD') with domain-specific terms in each of the ten thematic areas; the search strategy, comprising the core terms and the domain-specific term sets, is documented in Supplementary Material S2.
Reference lists of retained reviews and meta-analyses were hand-searched for additional sources.

Searches were conducted by a single reviewer without a pre-registered protocol; selection criteria were applied consistently but were not formalized prospectively, and this is stated as a limitation in §8.1.

Sources were included if published in peer-reviewed journals between 2006 and 2025; reporting an empirical or synthesized association between a candidate factor and ASD diagnosis, symptom severity, or a prospectively validated ASD-predictive marker; using human samples; and written in English or Spanish.

Sources were excluded if they were animal-model studies without human validation, except where cited solely to describe a proposed mechanism and identified as such; case reports or series with fewer than ten participants; reports of general developmental delay without ASD-specific outcome ascertainment; studies of intervention efficacy rather than risk, marker, or mechanism; or conference abstracts, dissertations, or non-peer-reviewed preprints.
Where publications reported overlapping samples, the most recent or comprehensive was retained.
Each retained source was mapped to one of 75 candidate risk factors and, through those factors, to a primary MERA domain and an evidential tier as defined in §5.1.
Sources were further classified along two dimensions.

The first was study design, in six categories: systematic review or meta-analysis; quantitative observational study, encompassing cohort, registry, prospective longitudinal, and case-control designs; theoretical or narrative review; qualitative study; idiographic or singlecase study; and mixed-methods study.
The second was journal indexing quartile at retrieval.

Where a journal was indexed in more than one database, the quartile from the database applying the more selective inclusion standard was retained, with Web of Science treated as the reference standard; 144 of the 152 pairings were classified from Web of Science and the remainder from Scopus or PubMed.

Indexing quartile does not constitute formal risk-of-bias assessment and is not presented as such; it is a coarse but transparent indicator of publication standard, to be weighed alongside the design distribution.
Correspondence between each source and the claim it was cited to support was independently verified before inclusion.
The classification is reported in Tables 1 and 2 and, at factor level, in Supplementary Table S1.

text.text: Because sources were not weighted by methodological quality and no pooled effect estimation was performed, the counts reported in §4 index the volume of available evidence per domain rather than the strength of association.
They should be read as a map of where evidence has accumulated, not as a ranking of effect magnitude.
A domain supported by many cross-sectional studies may carry less inferential weight than a domain supported by a single well-powered registry analysis.

Moving from volume to weight would require three steps not undertaken here: formal risk-of-bias appraisal of each source using design-appropriate instruments, extraction of comparable effect estimates with their precision, and random-effects pooling within factors where the underlying constructs are commensurable.
These steps constitute the planned second phase of the present research programme, and the domain weights they would yield are a precondition for any scoring algorithm derived from the framework.

text.text: Ten factors are supported by a single source, and a further subset by sources of one design type; these are identified as provisional.

Explicit identification of weakly supported components is a necessary condition for responsible operationalization: such factors should not enter a derived instrument without prior replication, and their inclusion here rests on theoretical coherence rather than established evidential weight.
Their retention reflects the function of a conceptual framework, which is to map the space of plausible signals so it can subsequently be pruned empirically.
MERA organizes empirically supported ASD-relevant signals into ten distinct but interrelated domains.

This is not a checklist of isolated predictors but a framework grounded in the premise that detection-relevant information is distributed across developmental windows and differs systematically in the inference it supports (Figure 2).
text.formatted: This is not a checklist of isolated predictors but a framework grounded in the premise that detection-relevant information is distributed across developmental windows and differs systematically in the inference it supports (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The components organized within MERA are not epistemologically homogeneous.
Some are antecedent exposures that cannot, by temporal logic, be consequences of the condition.
Others are early behavioural divergences that prospectively predict later diagnosis.
Others still are features of the diagnostic phenotype itself, or associated conditions whose direction of effect remains contested.
Treating these as a single category of risk factor would be conceptually imprecise and clinically misleading.
A four-tier classification of evidential status is therefore introduced, applied transversally across the ten domains.
Exposures or characteristics established before the developmental period in which an ASD phenotype could manifest, and which therefore cannot be consequences of the condition.

This tier comprises family psychiatric and neurological history and genetic syndromes (D1), obstetric and perinatal conditions (D2), prenatal toxic and pharmacological exposures (D3), congenital and neonatal medical events (part of D4), and antenatal maternal stress and depression (prenatal component of D10).
Evidence derives predominantly from population registries, birth cohorts, and genetically informed designs.
Function: risk stratification before any behavioural observation is possible.
Tier II -Early prodromal markers.

Behavioural or developmental divergences that emerge before the diagnostic threshold is reached and that prospectively predict later ASD outcome in longitudinal designs with pre-diagnostic measurement.

This tier comprises reduced canonical babbling and motor developmental delay (D5), diminished response to name, atypical gaze dynamics, and reduced joint attention (D6), and early repetitive engagement with objects (infant component of D7).
Evidence derives from prospective infant-sibling cohorts.
Function: extension of the detection window earlier than the eighteen-month anchor of current instruments.
These markers are behavioural, not pre-behavioural; their value lies in timing rather than modality.
Manifestations of the ASD phenotype itself, including features that constitute DSM-5 diagnostic criteria.
This tier comprises consolidated restricted and repetitive behaviours (D7) and atypical sensory reactivity (D8, corresponding to DSM-5 criterion B4).
Evidence derives from case-control and cross-sectional designs.
Function: case identification and phenotypic characterisation.
These features are explicitly not risk factors; their inclusion carries no aetiological claim.
Conditions cooccurring with ASD at elevated rates whose direction of effect is contested, plausibly reciprocal, or confounded by shared antecedents.

This tier comprises epilepsy, anaemia, and autoimmune conditions (part of D4), gastrointestinal dysfunction and food selectivity (D9), and postnatal maternal depression, adverse childhood experiences, and early screen exposure (postnatal component of D10).
Function: clinical flags that raise the index of suspicion and warrant comprehensive assessment, without supporting causal attribution.

text.text: Two implications follow.
First, the tiers carry different inferential weights, and any instrument derived from MERA must weight them differentially rather than summing them as equivalent units.

Second, the cumulative-risk logic set out in §6.1 applies with full force only within Tier I. Across Tiers II to IV, accumulation indexes increasing evidence of an emerging or established phenotype rather than increasing aetiological load-a distinction that must be preserved in any scoring algorithm derived from the framework.
The classification invites an objection that is better stated than left implicit.
If the components of Tiers III and IV are not risk factors-if some are diagnostic criteria and others are of contested directionality-what remains of a framework designated as a risk architecture?
And is it not circular to detect autism partly by observing autism?
The objection rests on a conflation of two functions that clinical detection instruments routinely combine, and the combination is neither novel nor problematic.

The neonatal early-onset sepsis calculator is an instructive precedent: it establishes a prior probability of infection from antenatal and intrapartum maternal factors alone-gestational age, maternal intrapartum temperature, duration of membrane rupture, group B streptococcus status, and intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (Puopolo et al., 2011; Escobar et al., 2014)-and then updates that prior against the infant's concurrent clinical examination, classified as well-appearing, equivocal, or clinically ill, to yield a posterior probability that guides management (Kuzniewicz et al., 2017).

text.text: No one regards this two-stage structure as circular.
The antecedent information identifies which infants warrant closer observation; the concurrent signs determine what that observation finds.
The two classes of information answer different questions and are combined by design rather than by conceptual error.
MERA operates on the same logic, and the four-tier taxonomy makes the division of labour explicit.

Tiers I and II perform an anticipatory function: they identify elevated probability before a consolidated phenotype exists-Tier I before any behaviour can be observed, and Tier II before the diagnostic threshold is reached.
Tiers III and IV perform a confirmatory and characterising function: in a child already flagged by the preceding tiers, they raise posterior probability and describe the presentation.

What the framework prohibits-and what an unclassified list of risk factors would fail to prohibit-is the use of Tier III or IV information as evidence of aetiological risk, or its inclusion in a prospective risk calculation as though it were antecedent.
The contribution should therefore be stated precisely.
It does not lie in the individual factors, most of which are separately established.

It lies in three things: the temporal stratification of heterogeneous signals according to when each becomes clinically observable; the explicit specification of what inference each class can bear; and the proposal that these signals be aggregated into a single evolving risk profile rather than evaluated independently at one screening point.
Whether that aggregation improves detection is an empirical question this paper does not claim to answer.
Overlap between domains is genuine and warrants explicit treatment.

Several factors appear substantively in more than one domain: oral-motor and swallowing difficulties bridge early medical conditions (D4) and feeding (D9); food texture rejection bridges sensory reactivity (D8) and feeding selectivity (D9); dietary exposure to additives and preserved foods bridges toxic exposure (D3) and feeding (D9); maternal depression bridges perinatal conditions (D2) and psychosocial context (D10); gesture and motor imitation bridge psychomotor development (D5) and social behaviour (D6); and visual fascination with repetitive movement bridges restricted behaviours (D7) and sensory processing (D8).
This overlap is informative rather than a defect of the classification.
The principle of interactive amplification set out in §6.1 predicts precisely this pattern: where shared biological pathways link domains, phenotypic expression should cross domain boundaries.
Domain overlap is on this reading a corollary of the model rather than an inconsistency within it.
It nonetheless carries a measurement consequence the framework must address directly.
In any instrument derived from MERA, cross-listed factors must be assigned to a single primary domain to prevent doublecounting and consequent inflation of cumulative risk estimates.

MERA is therefore characterized more precisely as a neurodevelopmental risk architecture with ASD-oriented weighting rather than as an ASD-exclusive model.

Tier I. The components of this domain are antecedent by definition: family history and genetic constitution precede the child's development and cannot be consequences of an emerging phenotype.
Evidence derives predominantly from population registries and genetically informed designs; 12 of the 15 sources in this domain are quartile-1 publications.
The heritability of ASD is among the highest of any neurodevelopmental condition, with twin studies estimating monozygotic concordance of 64-91%.

Its genetic architecture is highly polygenic, involving hundreds of common variants of small effect alongside rare de novo mutations, and a critical implication is that genetic risk extends well beyond ASD itself to a broad neuropsychiatric phenotype.
Population-based studies demonstrate that family history of ADHD is associated with elevated ASD likelihood, consistent with shared genetic aetiology (Rommelse et al., 2010; van Steijn et al., 2012).

Obstetric and perinatal conditions are antecedent by temporal logic.

Maternal depression is split: antenatal depression is Tier I, whereas postpartum depression is assigned to Tier IV, since an emerging infant phenotype may plausibly contribute to maternal depressive symptoms.
This is the largest domain in the evidence base ( 26pairings across 12 factors) and among the most heavily supported by pooled estimates: 11 of its sources are systematic reviews or meta-analyses.

text.text: Advanced maternal age is among the most replicated findings in this domain.

Al-Salihy (2025) reported that maternal age was the dominant predictor in an ecological model of ASD prevalence across two decades of population data; the design is ecological and the estimate should not be read as an individual-level effect.

Busque et al. (2022) reported an adjusted odds ratio of 2.22 for maternal age of 35 years or above in a cohort restricted to infants born before 29 weeks of gestation; the association is therefore established within an extremely preterm population and its generalisation to term births is not established by that study.

Advanced paternal age independently contributes through accumulation of de novo mutations in spermatogonial cells (Bozkurt et al., 2025), who also reported that paternal age and a history of hypoxia or asphyxia were associated with greater symptom severity rather than diagnosis alone.

Song, A. Y. et al. (2022) showed that accelerated parental epigenetic age-biological rather than chronological-was associated with lower cognitive outcomes and elevated ASD likelihood, while decelerated paternal epigenetic ageing was associated with reduced likelihood.
Caesarean delivery has received increasing attention.

A meta-analysis of 35 studies found a significant association with ASD (OR = 1.25), particularly pronounced for caesarean with general anaesthesia (OR = 1.62), and reported a parallel association with ADHD (Chen et al., 2024).
Liu et al. (2022) confirmed this in over 1.4 million low-risk California births, estimating that up to 10% of cases may be attributable to unnecessary caesarean delivery.
Proposed mechanisms include microbiome disruption, anaesthetic exposure, and altered stress hormone activation.
Gestational hypertension and preeclampsia represent another well-documented area, and the evidence distinguishes between the two more sharply than the domain label suggests.
Curran et al. (2018) reported approximately double the odds of ASD in offspring of mothers with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in the UK Millennium Cohort.
Maher et al. (2020), in a Swedish population-based study, reported an elevation of the order of 25 percent for preeclampsia specifically.

Separately, and in an experimental rather than epidemiological design, Curran et al. (2018) observed that serum from preeclamptic pregnancies altered neuronal growth in vitro; this is consistent with a neurobiological pathway but does not establish that it accounts for the epidemiological association.
Xie, Q. et al. (2020) identified 156 genes common to preeclampsia and ASD, including RPS4Y1, proposed as relevant to male preponderance.
The heterogeneity of estimates across hypertensive conditions suggests these may warrant separate treatment in a later iteration (see §8.2).

Gestational diabetes mellitus is associated with a 30-31 percent increase in ASD likelihood across meta-analyses (Garza-Martínez et al., 2025; Guo, D. et al., 2025), with risk amplified when pharmacological treatment was required during pregnancy.

text.text: Tier I. Prenatal exposures are antecedent by definition.
This domain also contains the components of the framework most plausibly modifiable through public health action, and is therefore of particular relevance to prevention as distinct from detection.
Ten of its 21 pairings derive from systematic reviews or meta-analyses, the highest proportion of any domain.
The developing brain is highly sensitive to exogenous chemical exposures during critical periods of prenatal neurogenesis, migration, and synaptogenesis.
Mixed: Tier I and Tier IV.

Congenital and neonatal events-prematurity, neonatal infection, congenital hypothyroidism-are antecedent and belong to Tier I. Epilepsy, anaemia, and autoimmune conditions are assigned to Tier IV: their temporal relation to ASD is frequently concurrent or subsequent, and reverse or reciprocal pathways are plausible.
Prematurity is one of the most robust medical risk factors.

Chang et al. (2023) demonstrated in a nationwide Taiwanese cohort that infants born before 28 weeks had a fourfold elevated risk of ASD with intellectual disability, rising progressively as gestational age decreased; Guo et al. (2024) confirmed this by meta-analysis.
Nagai et al. (2024) documented that primitive reflex persistence in very low birth weight infants was associated with later diagnosis, suggesting a neurological pathway.
Severe bacterial infections with hospitalization have been associated with a hazard ratio of 13.80 for ASD (Hsu et al., 2022).

text.text: Tier II, with concurrent components.
Motor delay, reduced canonical babbling, and regression are prospectively measured before diagnosis in infant-sibling cohorts and constitute prodromal markers.
Echolalia, perseverative speech, and comprehension difficulties are concurrent features that presuppose a developmental level not present in infancy, and belong to Tier III.
The assumption that ASD is primarily a disorder of social communication has obscured the extent to which motor development is systematically atypical from early infancy.

Prospective studies using standardized motor assessments have consistently documented delays in sitting, crawling, and walking at rates significantly higher than population norms. Hedgecock et al. (2018) demonstrated that gross motor delay modulates quality of life and behavioral outcomes. Gabis et al. (2020) showed that motor delay is a more frequent early red flag in girls than previously recognized, with implications for the female phenotype, whose social communication deficits are often subtler-making motor atypicality a more accessible early marker in this population. Stachura et al. (2025), using the MABC-2, confirmed coordination, balance, and fine motor deficits in children without co-occurring conditions.

(2024), in a prospective study using monthly all-day recordings from birth to 13 months, found reduced canonical babbling ratios from approximately 9 months in infants later diagnosed with ASD, with the effect concentrated among boys; girls later diagnosed did not show reduced rates relative to neurotypical girls, and the sex-specific character of this marker constrains its use as a universal screening indicator. text.text: Tier II.
The markers in this domain are behavioural and therefore observable, but they emerge months before the diagnostic threshold is reached and are measured prospectively in highlikelihood infant cohorts.
Their contribution lies in timing rather than in modality.
Emotion recognition is an exception, belonging to Tier III.

Physical contact avoidance has neurobiological grounding. Kadlaskar et al. (2019) showed that infants at high likelihood for ASD show atypical responses to caregiver touch, with reduced or aversive responses predictive of later social communication difficulties, and Smirni et al. (2019) reviewed tactile defensiveness in neurodevelopmental disorders, placing physical contact avoidance at the intersection of social and sensory domains.

text.text: Mixed: Tier II and Tier III.
Repetitive engagement with objects at nine months is prospectively predictive and belongs to Tier II.
Consolidated restricted and repetitive behaviours constitute DSM-5 criterion B and belong to Tier III: they are features of the diagnostic phenotype and are not risk factors.
Their function within the framework is confirmatory, not anticipatory.
Tier III.
Sensory hyper-and hyporeactivity corresponds to DSM-5 criterion B4 and is therefore constitutive of the diagnostic phenotype rather than antecedent to it.
Its inclusion reflects utility for case identification and phenotypic characterisation, and carries no aetiological claim.

Sensory processing differences are present in an estimated 69-93% of individuals with ASD and, while not included as a diagnostic criterion until DSM-5, are increasingly recognized as a central feature of the condition rather than a secondary symptom. Scheerer et al. (2021) identified five distinct sensory phenotypes through cluster analysis, including a taste-and-smell sensitivity phenotype, supporting the view that sensory differences are heterogeneous across the spectrum and require domain-specific assessment.

Baweja et al. (2023) documented high prevalence of exaggerated physical reactions, including self-injury, in ASD compared to ADHD and population controls, while Ferguson et al. (2025) reviewed the mechanisms underlying self-injurious behaviours in ASD with profound intellectual disability.

Crucially, sensory hypersensitivity in infants is observable and reportable by caregivers before behavioral and communication signs emerge; the inclusion of sensory markers therefore extends the detection window and captures a dimension of ASD that is both clinically significant and informative about underlying neurocircuitry differences.
Tier IV.
Gastrointestinal dysfunction and food selectivity co-occur with ASD at elevated rates, but the direction of effect is contested and in several instances explicitly reciprocal.

These components function as clinical flags warranting comprehensive assessment; they do not support aetiological attribution and should not enter a prospective risk calculation as antecedent factors.
With 7 pairings across 3 factors this is the smallest domain in the evidence base.

Attachment quality, adverse childhood experiences, and early screen exposure are assigned to Tier IV: for each, reverse causation is plausible, since an emerging phenotype may shape dyadic interaction, vulnerability to adversity, and patterns of screen use.

text.text: These findings are consistent with two interpretations the available designs cannot distinguish.

Screen exposure may amplify neurodevelopmental vulnerability by displacing reciprocal social interaction; alternatively, and equally consistent with the data, an emerging autistic phenotype may itself increase screen engagement, whether through the child's preference for predictable visual stimuli or through caregivers' use of screens to manage behavioural difficulty.
This component is accordingly assigned to Tier IV, and no causal reading is advanced.
The ten domains described above are not independent risk factors to be summed in a linear checklist.
MERA conceives of ASD vulnerability as an emergent property of cumulative, interactive risk across biological, developmental, environmental, and relational dimensions.
Three theoretical principles organize the model, as illustrated in Figure 3.
text.formatted: Three theoretical principles organize the model, as illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_10">3</ref>.

text.text: The principle of cumulative vulnerability holds that the probability of ASD increases non-linearly as risk factors accumulate across domains.

A child who experienced prenatal paracetamol exposure, maternal gestational hypertension, perinatal hypoxia, neonatal infection requiring hospitalization, and early microbiome disruption occupies a qualitatively different risk position than a child with any one of these factors in isolation.

The principle of temporal stratification recognizes that risk factors operate across distinct developmental windows with differential neurological sensitivity: prenatal toxic exposures during the first trimester affect cortical neurogenesis; third-trimester obstetric complications affect migration and synaptogenesis; neonatal medical events affect early circuit formation; and early psychosocial factors shape attachment and social brain development.

The principle of interactive amplification holds that risk factors across domains potentiate each other through shared biological pathwaysneuroinflammation, epigenetic reprogramming, and microbiome-brain signaling-rather than merely through statistical artifact.
The three principles are advanced as testable propositions rather than as established findings.
No dataset currently exists in which all ten domains have been measured within a single cohort, and consequently none of the three has been tested in the integrated form proposed here.
Each generates a specific and falsifiable prediction.

Cumulative vulnerability predicts that a multiplicative or threshold model of cross-domain accumulation will outperform an additive model in predicting ASD outcome in prospective cohorts; the cumulative-risk tradition in developmental psychopathology provides established analytic methods for such model comparison, and if an additive model performs equivalently or better, the principle is refuted.

Temporal stratification predicts that the predictive weight of a given factor will vary systematically as a function of the developmental window in which it occurs-that first-trimester and third-trimester exposure to the same agent will carry measurably different effect sizes-and is refuted by the finding that timing does not moderate effect.

Interactive amplification predicts statistical interaction terms of specified sign between designated domain pairs: between polygenic risk (D1) and prenatal toxicant exposure (D3); between early antibiotic exposure (D4) and gastrointestinal dysfunction (D9); and between caregiver-infant interaction quality (D10) and sensory reactivity (D8).
These are testable as interaction effects in adequately powered cohorts, and their absence refutes the principle.

The principles are the model's hypotheses, not its findings, and the framework should be evaluated on the coherence and testability of those hypotheses rather than on evidence it does not yet possess.
MERA is theoretically consonant with several existing frameworks in developmental psychopathology.

The multiple-hit hypothesis, originally formulated for schizophrenia, holds that neurodevelopmental disorders result from the accumulation of multiple genetic and environmental insults rather than from a single causal event, with an early priming insult increasing vulnerability to a subsequent one (Bayer et al., 1999; Maynard et al., 2001).

text.text: Applied to ASD, this model predicts the phenotypic heterogeneity observed clinically and the variable penetrance of individual risk factors across individuals.

text.text: A reasonable objection to MERA is that general developmental surveillance already captures much of what Tier II describes.

The Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3), the Survey of Well-being of Young Children (SWYC), and the periodic surveillance recommended by paediatric guidelines all evaluate gross and fine motor milestones, expressive and receptive language, and elements of social-emotional development from the first year of life.
The added value of MERA must therefore be stated precisely rather than assumed.
Three contributions can be identified.

The first, and most substantive, concerns Tier I. These data are already generated in routine perinatal and paediatric care-obstetric records, birth parameters, neonatal event logs, family history-but are not aggregated into any developmental risk profile and are not consulted when a concern subsequently arises.
MERA proposes integrating information that already exists in the clinical record, a substantially lower implementation burden than new data collection.

The second concerns sequencing: MERA specifies which classes of signal are informative at which window, permitting temporally stratified rather than uniform surveillance, whereas existing instruments are milestone-referenced but not risk-stratified.
The third concerns scoring logic: cumulative cross-tier accumulation rather than independent pass-or-fail evaluation of discrete milestones.

Where Tier II overlaps with existing surveillance, this is an implementation asset rather than redundancy, indicating that a substantial component can be operationalized through instruments already embedded in primary care-a consideration of importance in health systems, including Chile's, where parallel screening infrastructure is not realistic.
Rather than a single behavioral checklist at 18 months, MERA suggests tiered surveillance in which domains are assessed at windows corresponding to their biological and behavioral salience.

Prenatally and at birth, Domains 1-3 can be assessed through routine antenatal records and family history; during the first year, Domains 4-6, 8, and 10 become assessable through caregiver report and structured surveillance; after 12 months, Domains 6, 7, and 9 become fully assessable through both caregiver report and direct observation.
This would enable progressive accumulation of a multidomain risk profile, earlier identification before behavioral signs consolidate, and more targeted use of specialist resources.

It also opens the path toward predictive models-weighted risk calculators, machine learning classifiers, or Bayesian networks-trained on prospective multidomain data, moving beyond screening toward genuine risk stratification.
>Clinical and Public Health Implications
text.formatted: <head n="7." >Clinical and Public Health Implications</head>

text.text: MERA has concrete implications for primary care that can be implemented without waiting for new validated instruments.

Paediatricians, midwives, and family practitioners managing prenatal care and well-child visits are positioned to collect multidomain risk information across Domains 1-4 as part of standard documentation.

Integrating a brief family neuropsychiatric history, systematic recording of obstetric complications, and standardized neonatal records into a developmental risk profile would cost little clinical time but could substantially advance the detection timeline.

Identification of multiple risk factors across Domains 1-4 could trigger enhanced surveillance in Domains 5-10 during the first two years-a tiered approach analogous to risk-stratified surveillance in neonatology.
In Chile, the epidemiological and policy context makes early ASD detection an urgent public health priority.

Diagnostic delays of two to four years from first parental concern to formal diagnosis are common, meaning children who could benefit from early intervention are frequently not identified until school age, when the neuroplasticity window is substantially reduced.

The Chilean public health system conducts universal developmental assessments during the first years of life through primary care; these contact points represent existing infrastructure that could be leveraged for multidomain risk surveillance without requiring a parallel specialist system.

The Chilean context also introduces locally relevant risk modifiers-industrial contamination in specific regions, high consumption of processed and canned foods, patterns of maternal healthcare access, and psychosocial stressors associated with economic inequality and migration-warranting investigation in Chilean cohort studies.

Ethical implementation of any MERA-derived instrument must be equity-oriented, avoiding stigmatization of families whose risk circumstances reflect social determinants rather than individual failures.
The probabilistic nature of risk must be clearly communicated: multiple factors increase probability but do not determine outcome, and many high-likelihood children will not develop ASD.
Premature labeling without careful clinical assessment risks unnecessary parental anxiety and unjustified intervention.
The framework reorganizes a body of evidence that is largely established but not previously integrated.

Its claim is not that the factors are new, but that their temporal stratification, classification by evidential status, and aggregation into one evolving profile constitute a detection architecture current instruments do not provide.
This section sets out the limitations qualifying that claim and the agenda following from it.
Several limitations should be acknowledged transparently.

First, the evidence base was organized through a narrative rather than a systematic review with formal PRISMA procedures, which introduces the possibility of selection bias and limits the precision with which differential weights can be assigned across domains.

For a theoretical integration across ten heterogeneous domains, a narrative approach permits the conceptual synthesis that a strict PRISMA-constrained review would preclude-a tradeoff that is methodologically defensible at this stage of model development -but searches were conducted by a single reviewer without a pre-registered protocol, and sources that were never retrieved could not be assessed.
Future work should formalize the search strategy through prospective registration and apply the meta-analytic procedures described in §3.5.

Second, the empirical literature underlying MERA draws predominantly on population cohort studies from Northern European, North American, and East Asian contexts; the applicability of the proposed domain structure and weights to Latin American populations-including Chile, where this research programme is anchored-remains to be empirically established, and cultural, dietary, and environmental factors specific to these contexts may warrant additional domains or item reformulation.
Third, MERA is at present a conceptual architecture rather than a validated psychometric instrument.

While the ten-domain structure is empirically grounded, its clinical utility-including sensitivity, specificity, and predictive value-cannot be confirmed until prospective cohort studies with paired samples test the framework against behavioural outcomes.

This limitation is deliberate and methodologically appropriate: conceptual frameworks precede instrumentation, and the framework was developed explicitly as the foundation for a structured validation programme.
A multidomain caregiver-report instrument derived from the framework has been constructed and has entered content validation through expert judgement.

It includes the factors identified in §4.4 as provisionally supported; this is deliberate, since the expert-judgement procedure and the subsequent factor-analytic stage are designed to evaluate rather than to presuppose the adequacy of each item, and factors that fail to meet retention criteria will be removed before the instrument enters predictive validation.

Fourth, the proposed cross-domain interactions-the amplification pathways mediated by neuroinflammation, the gut-brain microbiome axis, and epigenetic reprogramming-are grounded in converging biological evidence but remain inferential at the level of individual domain combinations; their formal characterisation will require mechanistic studies and computational modelling on prospective datasets.

Fifth, the domain structure and factor granularity constitute a conceptual partition whose empirical validity is an open question; a factor solution obtained in validation samples is expected to depart from the present structure.
These limitations define rather than undermine the framework's contribution: they constitute the empirical agenda through which a model of this scope is translated into clinical practice.
MERA generates several research priorities: prospective longitudinal studies in Chilean and Latin

American populations to test whether the domain structure and risk weights generalize beyond predominantly Northern European and North American samples; instrument development to operationalize the framework into validated caregiver-report and clinician-administered tools, with particular attention to the prenatal and first-year domains unaddressed by existing instruments; intervention research to determine whether risk-stratified surveillance improves outcomes over standard behavioral screening; and mechanistic research to characterize the pathways through which cross-domain interactions operate.
A second class of priority concerns the granularity of the factor structure itself, which is in several places demonstrably coarser than the evidence it organizes.
Four refinements are sufficiently well specified to state concretely.

Maternal and paternal age are currently treated as a single parentalage factor, but the literature comprises studies examining each independently and studies examining them jointly, with different effect structures; these warrant disaggregation.

The syndromic component of Domain 1 is represented at a granularity that the comparative evidence does not support, since symptom profiles differ systematically across fragile X syndrome, Angelman syndrome, tuberous sclerosis complex, and neurofibromatosis type 1 (Lubbers et al., 2024).

text.text: A third priority concerns sex differences, which recur across domains in a pattern the present framework does not model.

Canonical babbling is reduced in boys later diagnosed with ASD but not in girls (Long et al., 2024); motor delay is a more prevalent early indicator in girls (Gabis et al., 2020); BTEX exposure is associated with differential incidence by sex (Hashemi et al., 2025); and dietary mercury exposure shows sex-dependent association (O'Connor et al., 2025).

text.text: Whether sex operates as a moderator of individual factor weights, as a determinant of which markers are informative, or both, is a question that a multidomain framework is well positioned to address and that single-factor studies cannot.
This is the most substantive extension available to the framework and a principal objective of its next iteration.
By anchoring detection to the behavioural signs that consolidate at eighteen months and later, current frameworks miss two distinct classes of information.

The first is a genuinely prebehavioural set of antecedent risk markers-genetic, obstetric, toxicological, and early medicalthat are established before any behavioural phenotype could be observed, and that are therefore inaccessible to any instrument, however early, that relies on observation of the child.

The second is a set of early behavioural divergences in psychomotor, communicative, social, and sensory functioning which are themselves observable, but which emerge months before the diagnostic threshold is reached and are consequently not captured by instruments calibrated to the eighteenmonth window.
The distinction matters for what follows from it.

The first class extends detection into a period in which no behavioural observation is possible, and can be addressed only by aggregating biomedical and family-history information already held in the clinical record.

The second extends detection into a period in which behaviour is observable but is not currently being observed, and can be addressed by earlier and more targeted use of instruments that already exist.
These are different problems with different solutions.
At the same time, the phenotypic expansion of ASD underscores that even behavioural detection frameworks may be calibrated too narrowly.
The Multidomain Early Risk Architecture proposed here represents a conceptually grounded response to these limitations.

By organizing ten empirically supported domains into a developmentally stratified structure, by classifying their components according to evidential status, and by formulating the principles of cumulative vulnerability, temporal stratification, and interactive amplification as falsifiable hypotheses, MERA provides a foundation for the next generation of ASD early detection research and instrumentation.

Its implementation in primary care contexts-particularly in settings such as Chile where diagnostic delays impose substantial individual and social costs-has the potential to reduce the gap between the emergence of detectable signals and access to intervention.
The path from this conceptual framework to a validated multidomain instrument is the most urgent priority for the research programme it inaugurates.

For clinical implementation, elevated cumulative risk within Tiers I and IV should trigger comprehensive neurodevelopmental surveillance rather than ASD-specific screening.

For validation design, prospective testing of MERA should evaluate the framework against a range of neurodevelopmental outcomes rather than against ASD alone.

(2024)</ref> found that early gestural development significantly predicted subsequent symptom severity.

text.text: Restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) constitute one of the two core DSM-5 criteria and encompass sensorimotor repetitions, insistence on sameness, circumscribed interests, and ritualistic routines.

Early forms are detectable at 9 months: Miller et al. (2021) showed that repetitive behavior with objects at 9 months predicts later diagnosis and social behavioral severity, and Song, D.-Y. et al. (2022) documented RRB patterns in toddlers by factor analysis, identifying subtypes including insistence on sameness and sensorimotor repetitions.
Fixation on spinning objects is well documented.

Kirby et al. (2015) found sensory interests including spinning fixation more frequent and complex in ASD than in other groups; Chen et al. (2022) documented preferential visual attention to non-social repetitive stimuli by eye-tracking; Wang et al. (2018) showed experimentally a preference for repetitive over random movements; and Omori (2025) showed increased observation of predictable visual stimuli, a measurable screening signal.
Mehralizadeh et al. (2023) developed a sensorized toy car using spinning object interest as a screening feature.

Object lining is specifically distinctive: Greaves et al. (2006) confirmed it as ASD-characteristic against Prader-Willi syndrome; McDermott et al. (2020) validated measurement subcategories in adolescents and adults; and Li et al. (2021) showed that heterogeneity in visual preferences may reflect distinct sensorimotor subtypes.Circumscribed interests are distinguished not primarily by intensity but by unusual content and their competition with social stimuli for attentional resources.Burrows et al. (2021) found that toddlers' interests are more peculiar in content rather than necessarily more intense than those of typically developing peers, andWang et al. (2021) demonstrated experimentally that circumscribed interests modulate eye contact in boys with ASD, providing a mechanistic link between RRBs and social behavioral features.

text.text: difficulties and gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms are significantly more prevalent in ASD than in the general population and are among the most impairing comorbidities.

McElhanon et al. (2014) found elevated rates of diarrhea (OR = 3.63) and constipation (OR = 3.86) by meta-analysis, and Lasheras et al. (2023) confirmed GI prevalence across diverse cultural contexts.

The bidirectionality defining this domain's tier assignment is documented directly: Akama et al. (2025) found distinct psychiatric features including greater anxiety and behavioral rigidity in children with ASD and chronic functional constipation, suggesting reciprocal brain-gut interactions, and Li et al. (2024) showed that dietary intake and GI symptoms relate to ASD-linked traits bidirectionally rather than causally.
Jafari et al. (2022) documented GI symptom profiles, and Manzi et al. (2008) proposed that metabolic disorders with GI manifestations may contribute through disrupted biochemical pathways.
Breastfeeding difficulties in early infancy have been associated with ASD.

Yuan et al. (2024), in a Chinese case-control study, reported an adjusted OR of 3.46 in children whose mothers reported breastfeeding difficulties, suggesting that early oral-motor difficulties may represent a detectable neonatal signal; Vasilakis et al. (2022) identified breastfeeding rejection and oral-motor difficulties as early signs warranting prospective investigation; and Şahan et al. (2021) found significant differences in solid food transition timing, tongue thrust, and mealtime behavioral organization.
Intense food selectivity-driven by sensory hypersensitivity to texture, odor, color, and temperature-affects up to 70% of children with ASD.

Zulkifli et al. (2022) reviewed 30 studies identifying oral sensory sensitivity as the central driver and documenting resulting nutritional deficiencies; Alibrandi et al. (2023) found texture, smell, color, and temperature to be primary rejection triggers in a Southern Italian sample; Rodrigues et al. (2023) confirmed greater selectivity versus neurotypical children with oral-atypical sensitivity as the key mechanism; and Ausderau et al. (2024) validated a factor structure encompassing sensory, behavioral, oral-motor, and gastrointestinal components.

MERA heuristic model: proposed cross-domain interaction and biological amplification pathways.

Domains are arranged in three concentric rings by temporal proximity to behavioural expression: outer ring (contextual and environmental: D1, D2, D3, D10), middle ring (biomedical: D4, D8, D9), and inner ring (developmental behavioural: D5, D6, D7).
Solid arrows indicate proposed direct amplification; dashed arrows indicate proposed bidirectional or modulating relationships.

The three biological axes represented-neuroinflammation, the gut-brain microbiome pathway, and epigenetic reprogramming-are proposed mechanistic hypotheses rather than established mediating relationships.
The figure is heuristic and is intended to specify testable interaction predictions, not to assert a demonstrated causal architecture.
